---
slug: top-k-flows
title: Top K Flows
difficulty: medium
patterns: [heap]
lists: [network-practice, ascend-150]
companies: [arista, cisco, cloudflare, nvidia]
order: 11
lesson: fabric-networking/operating-fabrics/telemetry-and-observability
hints:
  - "Two jobs hide in this problem. First add up the bytes per flow, where a flow is the ordered pair (src, dst). Only then rank the flows. Ranking the raw records gives the wrong answer as soon as one flow has several records."
  - "Sorting every flow costs O(m log m) for m flows. You only need k of them. A min-heap of size k keeps the k best seen so far, and its root is the weakest of them: the one a new, better flow pushes out."
  - "Write the comparison once, as \"a is worse than b\": fewer bytes is worse, and on equal bytes the larger (src, dst) is worse, because ties go to the smaller key. The heap's root must be the worst kept flow, so the heap orders by that rule. Pop everything at the end and reverse it."
signatures:
  python:
    name: top_k_flows
    starter: |
      def top_k_flows(records: list[list], k: int) -> list[list]:
          pass
  javascript:
    name: top_k_flows
    starter: |
      function top_k_flows(records, k) {
      }
tests:
  - args: [[["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 1500], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.2.20", 9000], ["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 64000], ["10.250.12.10", "10.250.14.10", 128], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.2.20", 9000], ["10.1.1.10", "203.0.113.10", 40000]], 2]
    expected: [["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 65500], ["10.1.1.10", "203.0.113.10", 40000]]
    label: "acme flows: aggregate per pair, two heaviest"
  - args: [[["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.10", 5000], ["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 3000], ["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 2000], ["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.11", 5000], ["192.0.2.200", "203.0.113.10", 4999]], 3]
    expected: [["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 5000], ["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.10", 5000], ["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.11", 5000]]
    label: "ties broken by (src, dst) ascending"
  - args: [[["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 7000], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 900], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 900], ["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 100]], 2]
    expected: [["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 7100], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 1800]]
    label: "each direction is its own flow"
  - args: [[["10.1.2.20", "10.1.1.10", 300], ["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 300]], 5]
    expected: [["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 300], ["10.1.2.20", "10.1.1.10", 300]]
    label: "k larger than the number of flows"
  - args: [[], 3]
    expected: []
    label: "no records"
  - args: [[["10.1.1.9", "10.1.2.20", 2048], ["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 2048], ["10.1.1.100", "10.1.2.20", 2048]], 2]
    expected: [["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 2048], ["10.1.1.100", "10.1.2.20", 2048]]
    hidden: true
    label: "ties compare as strings, not as numbers"
  - args: [[["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 500], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.2.20", 0], ["172.16.1.11", "172.16.0.5", 0]], 0]
    expected: []
    hidden: true
    label: "k = 0"
  - args: [[["172.16.1.11", "172.16.0.5", 0], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.2.20", 0], ["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 0]], 2]
    expected: [["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 0], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.2.20", 0]]
    hidden: true
    label: "zero-byte flows still count and still tie-break"
  - args: [[["10.250.1.10", "10.250.9.10", 1048576]], 1]
    expected: [["10.250.1.10", "10.250.9.10", 1048576]]
    label: "single record"
  - args: [[["10.250.9.10", "10.250.20.10", 9000], ["10.250.4.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.2.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.5.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.8.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.1.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.10.10", "10.250.20.10", 7000], ["10.250.7.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.3.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000], ["10.250.6.10", "10.250.20.10", 8000]], 4]

---
Every network operations dashboard has a "top talkers" panel: the handful of conversations carrying most of the bytes right now. When an uplink on `leaf2.ams` runs at 100%, the first question is whose traffic it is, and this panel answers it. This problem asks you to build the ranking behind it.

### The networking idea in one minute

A **flow** is one direction of a conversation between two endpoints. Routers and switches do not export every packet; they keep a small table of active flows and periodically export a **flow record** for each one, saying "between the last export and now, this source sent this many bytes to this destination". The standard formats are NetFlow (Cisco's original) and **IPFIX** (the IETF version, RFC 7011). Samplers such as sFlow produce estimates of the same thing from sampled packet headers. A collector receives these records from every device and adds them up.

Two facts about flow records shape this problem. First, one flow produces many records: a long transfer is reported once per export interval, so the collector must **sum per flow** before it can rank anything. Second, flows are **directional**: a database reply from `acme-db1` to `acme-web1` is a different flow from the query that went the other way, and usually much larger. Real flow keys are the full 5-tuple (addresses, ports, protocol) plus a tenant or VRF identifier; this problem keeps only the ordered pair of addresses.

Traffic is heavily skewed. A few **elephant flows** (a backup, a storage replication, a GPU collective) carry most of the bytes, and thousands of **mice** carry the rest. The top-k view is how an operator finds the elephants: the two that ECMP hashed onto the same uplink ([ECMP and hashing](/learn/fabric-networking/fabric-architecture/ecmp-and-hashing)), or the batch job that is filling a leaf's buffers.

The examples use Meridian's Acme hosts (`acme-web1` is `10.1.1.10`, `acme-web2` is `10.1.1.11`, `acme-db1` is `10.1.2.20`), Meridian's monitoring subnet `10.250.0.0/16` (probe agents and collectors), and the documentation ranges reserved for examples (`192.0.2.0/24`, `198.51.100.0/24`, `203.0.113.0/24`, RFC 5737).

### The task

Write `top_k_flows(records, k)`.

- `records` is a list of `[src, dst, bytes]`: two address strings and a non-negative integer. Several records may share the same `(src, dst)`.
- The **flow key** is the ordered pair `(src, dst)`. `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different flows.
- A flow's **total** is the sum of `bytes` over all its records. A flow whose records are all 0 bytes still exists, with total 0.

Return the `k` flows with the largest totals as a list of `[src, dst, total]`, heaviest first. When two flows have the same total, the one with the smaller key comes first: compare `src` as strings, then `dst` as strings. String comparison is deliberate (it is what a sorted table of keys does), so `"10.1.1.10"` sorts before `"10.1.1.9"`. If there are fewer than `k` flows, return all of them in that order. If `k` is 0, return an empty list.

Solve it without sorting every flow: keep only `k` candidates at a time.

### Examples

**Summing per flow.** Six records at Meridian's collector, `k = 2`:

| src | dst | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `10.1.1.10` | `10.1.2.20` | 1500 |
| `10.1.1.11` | `10.1.2.20` | 9000 |
| `10.1.1.10` | `10.1.2.20` | 64000 |
| `10.250.12.10` | `10.250.14.10` | 128 |
| `10.1.1.11` | `10.1.2.20` | 9000 |
| `10.1.1.10` | `203.0.113.10` | 40000 |

Output: `[["10.1.1.10", "10.1.2.20", 65500], ["10.1.1.10", "203.0.113.10", 40000]]`. The flow `acme-web1 → acme-db1` has two records, 1500 + 64000. `acme-web2 → acme-db1` has two records of 9000, for 18000, which loses to the single 40000-byte record. Ranking records instead of flows would pick the same two flows here but report the first as 64000, not 65500.

**Ties.** Records `["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.10", 5000]`, `["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 3000]`, `["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 2000]`, `["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.11", 5000]`, `["192.0.2.200", "203.0.113.10", 4999]`, `k = 3`.

Output: `[["192.0.2.33", "203.0.113.10", 5000], ["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.10", 5000], ["198.51.100.7", "203.0.113.11", 5000]]`. Three flows total 5000. `"192.0.2.33"` is the smallest source; the two `198.51.100.7` flows are ordered by destination. `192.0.2.200`, at 4999, misses by one byte.

**Direction matters.** Records `["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 7000]`, `["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 900]`, `["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 900]`, `["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 100]`, `k = 2`.

Output: `[["10.1.1.10", "10.1.1.11", 7100], ["10.1.1.11", "10.1.1.10", 1800]]`. The two directions are summed separately.

### Constraints

- `0 ≤ len(records) ≤ 10⁵`
- `0 ≤ bytes ≤ 10⁹` per record, so every total fits in a 64-bit integer and in a JavaScript number exactly.
- `0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁵`
- Addresses are non-empty strings of digits and dots.

### Follow-up

"The dashboard wants the top 10 flows **over the last 60 seconds**, refreshed every second, while records keep arriving. Records now carry a timestamp. How do you expire old bytes without re-adding the whole window each second? And when the collector sees 50 million distinct flows a minute and cannot hold a counter for each, what do you give up?"

## Solution

### The naive approach

Sum the records into a dictionary keyed by `(src, dst)`, then sort all `m` flows by `(-total, src, dst)` and take the first `k`. That is `O(n + m log m)` time and `O(m)` space, and it is correct. Say it first: in an interview it is the baseline, and with `m` in the thousands it is what you would ship. The cost that matters is the sort when `m` is large and `k` is small, which is the normal shape of a top-talkers query: a million flows, ten wanted.

An even more naive version sorts the *records* and takes the top `k`. It is wrong whenever one flow has several records, which in flow telemetry is always.

### The insight

Ranking is a selection problem, not a sorting problem. You never need the order of flow number 500 against flow number 501; you need to know whether a flow beats the weakest of the current best `k`. A **min-heap of size `k`** keeps exactly that: the best `k` seen so far, with the weakest at the root, readable in `O(1)` and replaceable in `O(log k)`.

The ordering is two-part, and both parts must point the same way. "Better" means more bytes, or equal bytes and a smaller key. The heap's root must be the *worst* kept flow, so the heap orders by "worse": fewer bytes, or equal bytes and a *larger* key. Getting the tie direction backwards is the classic bug here, because a plain `(bytes, src, dst)` tuple in a min-heap puts the smallest key at the root and evicts the flow that should have stayed.

### The optimal approach

1. One pass over the records adds each record's bytes to `totals[(src, dst)]`.
2. For each flow, wrap it in an object whose `<` means "is worse than". If the heap holds fewer than `k` items, push. Otherwise, if the heap's root is worse than this flow, replace the root.
3. Pop the heap until it is empty. Pops come out worst first, so reverse the list.

```python
import heapq


class _Flow:
    """A flow in the heap. `a < b` means "a is worse than b", so the heap's
    root is the weakest flow still in the top k."""
    __slots__ = ("total", "src", "dst")

    def __init__(self, total: int, src: str, dst: str):
        self.total, self.src, self.dst = total, src, dst

    def __lt__(self, other: "_Flow") -> bool:
        if self.total != other.total:
            return self.total < other.total               # fewer bytes is worse
        return (self.src, self.dst) > (other.src, other.dst)  # larger key loses a tie


def top_k_flows(records: list[list], k: int) -> list[list]:
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    totals: dict[tuple[str, str], int] = {}
    for src, dst, nbytes in records:
        totals[(src, dst)] = totals.get((src, dst), 0) + nbytes

    heap: list[_Flow] = []
    for (src, dst), total in totals.items():
        flow = _Flow(total, src, dst)
        if len(heap) < k:
            heapq.heappush(heap, flow)
        elif heap[0] < flow:                  # beats the weakest of the best k
            heapq.heapreplace(heap, flow)

    ranked = []
    while heap:
        f = heapq.heappop(heap)               # worst first
        ranked.append([f.src, f.dst, f.total])
    ranked.reverse()                          # heaviest first
    return ranked
```

Trace the tie example with `k = 3`. The totals are `198.51.100.7 → .10` 5000, `192.0.2.33 → .10` 5000, `198.51.100.7 → .11` 5000 and `192.0.2.200 → .10` 4999. The first three fill the heap. The root is the worst of the three: all have 5000, so the one with the largest key, `198.51.100.7 → .11`. The fourth flow has 4999, which is worse than the root, so it is skipped. Popping gives `.7 → .11`, then `.7 → .10`, then `192.0.2.33`; reversed, that is the expected output.

**Complexity.** Summing is `O(n)` expected time for `n` records. The selection pass does at most one `O(log k)` heap operation per flow, `O(m log k)` for `m` distinct flows, and draining is `O(k log k)`. Total `O(n + m log k)` time. Space is `O(m)` for the totals and `O(k)` for the heap; the totals dominate, and the follow-up is about that. When `k` is close to `m`, `O(m log k)` is no better than sorting, and sorting is simpler; say so.

### Common mistakes

- **Ranking records instead of flows.** The heap must see one entry per `(src, dst)` with its summed total. A flow with many small records is often the real elephant.
- **The tie in the wrong direction.** In a min-heap, the root is what gets evicted. If ties are ordered by ascending key, the root is the *smallest* key, which is the flow the problem says to keep.
- **Merging the two directions.** Keying on a sorted pair, or on a set of the two addresses, adds a request to its reply. Real flow records are unidirectional.
- **Forgetting the output order.** Draining a min-heap yields worst first. Reverse it, or fill the result from the back.
- **Numeric address order.** The problem compares keys as strings. Parsing addresses into integers for the tie-break changes the answer for `10.1.1.9` against `10.1.1.10`.
- **`k = 0` and `k > m`.** A size-0 heap that pushes before checking its size returns one flow; a loop that pops exactly `k` times fails when there are fewer flows.
- **JavaScript string keys.** Joining `src + dst` without a separator makes `"10.1.1.1" + "10.0.0.1"` and `"10.1.1.11" + "0.0.0.1"` the same string, `"10.1.1.110.0.0.1"`. Use a separator that cannot appear in an address, or nested maps.

### How to discuss it

Start by saying aloud that a flow appears in many records and that direction matters; that shows you know what flow telemetry is. Give the sort-everything baseline with its cost. Then: "I only need `k`, so a min-heap of size `k` whose root is the weakest kept flow; each flow either loses to the root or replaces it." State the comparison as one function and write it before the heap code, because the tie direction is where the bug lives. Mention that `heapq.nsmallest(k, totals.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))` does the same thing in one line, and that you wrote it out to show the mechanism. Finish with the complexity, the point where sorting is just as good (`k` close to `m`), and the observation that memory is dominated by the totals, which leads into the follow-up.

### The sliding window follow-up

Records now carry a timestamp, and the query is "top `k` over the last `W` seconds". Re-summing the window on every refresh costs `O(records in the window)` each second. Instead, keep the window as a ring of one-second buckets, each a small dictionary of per-flow bytes, plus one running `totals` dictionary. Adding a record updates its bucket and `totals`. When a bucket falls out of the window, subtract each of its entries from `totals` and delete flows that reach zero. Each record is added once and subtracted once, so maintenance is amortised `O(1)` per record, and a query is the same size-`k` heap over `totals`.

```python
import heapq
from collections import deque


class SlidingTopFlows:
    """Top flows over the last `window` seconds, in one-second buckets."""

    def __init__(self, window: int):
        self.window = window
        self.buckets: deque[tuple[int, dict]] = deque()   # (second, {key: bytes})
        self.totals: dict[tuple[str, str], int] = {}

    def _expire(self, now: int) -> None:
        while self.buckets and self.buckets[0][0] <= now - self.window:
            _, old = self.buckets.popleft()
            for key, nbytes in old.items():
                left = self.totals[key] - nbytes
                if left:
                    self.totals[key] = left
                else:
                    del self.totals[key]                    # no bytes left in the window

    def add(self, ts: int, src: str, dst: str, nbytes: int) -> None:
        self._expire(ts)
        if not self.buckets or self.buckets[-1][0] != ts:
            self.buckets.append((ts, {}))                   # timestamps arrive in order
        bucket = self.buckets[-1][1]
        bucket[(src, dst)] = bucket.get((src, dst), 0) + nbytes
        self.totals[(src, dst)] = self.totals.get((src, dst), 0) + nbytes

    def top(self, now: int, k: int) -> list[list]:
        self._expire(now)
        best = heapq.nsmallest(k, self.totals.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
        return [[src, dst, total] for (src, dst), total in best]
```

The parts to say out loud:

- **Granularity is a trade.** One-second buckets make the window exact to a second and cost `W` dictionaries. Coarser buckets (10 s) use less memory and make the window edge jumpy. A "hopping" window that just resets every minute is cheaper still and is what many dashboards actually draw.
- **Late and out-of-order records.** Exporters send on their own timers, and an IPFIX record describes an interval that already ended. Bucket by the record's flow-end time, accept records up to some lateness into older buckets, and drop or count anything later. The code above assumes order; say what you would change.
- **Query cost.** Each `top` is `O(m log k)` over the active flows. If the dashboard refreshes far more often than flows change, keep an ordered structure keyed by `(-total, src, dst)` (a balanced tree or skip list) and update it on every add and expire, so `top` is `O(k)` and each update `O(log m)`.
- **Memory when `m` is huge.** Fifty million distinct flows a minute is too many exact counters for one collector. The standard answer is a **heavy-hitters sketch**: Space-Saving keeps a fixed number of counters and, when a new flow arrives and all are taken, evicts the smallest and inherits its count, which guarantees that any flow above `total / counters` is kept; a Count-Min sketch plus a size-`k` heap gives overestimates with a bounded error. You give up exactness for the mice and keep it, approximately, for the elephants, which is the part the dashboard is for.

### Networking follow-ups

- **"What is the flow key really?"** The 5-tuple plus a tenant identifier. Meridian's Acme `acme-web1` and Globex `globex-app1` are both `10.1.1.10`; only the VRF or the VXLAN VNI (10100 against 10200) tells them apart. A collector that keys on the inner IP alone merges two customers' traffic into one "flow". The common wrong answer is "source and destination IP".
- **"The records are sampled."** sFlow samples 1 packet in N, so each sample stands for about N packets and the collector scales by N. Ranking is robust for elephants and noisy for mice; the [telemetry lesson](/learn/fabric-networking/operating-fabrics/telemetry-and-observability) works the error bars. Never present a flow estimated from a handful of samples as an exact byte count.
- **"Where do you aggregate?"** Every device exports, so the same flow is seen at the ingress leaf, a spine and the egress leaf. Summing across devices triple-counts it. Pick one observation point per flow (usually ingress at the leaf) or deduplicate by exporter and interface.
- **"Top flows on which link?"** The question during an incident is usually "who is on this congested uplink". Key by `(exporter, interface, flow)` and rank per interface; that is how you find two elephants that ECMP hashed onto one spine while another sits idle.
- **"Bytes or rate?"** Operators think in Gb/s. Divide the window total by the window length, and show the link's capacity next to it: a 40 Gb/s flow is noise on a 400G uplink and a crisis on a 10G one.
- **"AI fabrics."** RDMA traffic between GPUs is a few huge, long-lived flows per queue pair, all of similar size, so "top k" is less useful than "which flows share a link". The honest answer is that the platform should show per-link flow counts and imbalance as well as the ranking; the network team will know which collective is running.
